@graph.headline: Garbage In, Immutable Out: Where the Facts in a Verified Record Actually Come From
@graph.description: A ledger can prove a record has not changed since the day it was written. It cannot prove the record was true when it was written. Here is the input half of verifiable automation: the four questions any fact has to answer before it is worth anchoring, what an attestation actually proves, and why data freshness is a design parameter rather than a footnote.

mainEntity.name: Can a blockchain record be wrong?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Immutability guarantees the record has not changed since it was written; it says nothing about whether the fact was true when it went in. Input design matters more than the choice of ledger.

mainEntity.name: What is the oracle problem in plain English?

acceptedAnswer.text: A blockchain can only hold what is written to it and cannot fetch outside data on its own. Something has to carry the external fact in, and whatever carries it becomes the trust boundary. Choosing and hardening that carrier is the oracle problem.

mainEntity.name: Does one oracle node defeat the purpose?

acceptedAnswer.text: It reintroduces a single point of trust. Independent operators fetching independently and aggregating on-chain change the question from "who do you trust" to "how many parties would have to collude."

mainEntity.name: What does a data attestation actually prove?

acceptedAnswer.text: That a specific key signed a specific statement about specific bytes at a specific time. It does not prove the statement is accurate — acceptable, because most disputes are about who claimed what and when, not about the physics.

mainEntity.name: How do you verify a delivery or service record?

acceptedAnswer.text: Record the assertion at the point of completion — who, where, when, what — sign it, and anchor the hash so neither side can alter it later. Then set a validity window so a stale confirmation cannot be presented as a current one.
